# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven deep into workplace culture, that a good meeting is one where everyone leaves nodding. The room reaches agreement, heads bob, someone volunteers to "circle back," and everyone walks out feeling productive. But this picture of success deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, can be a mirage. It can mask confusion, unspoken doubts, and fundamental uncertainties that will resurface later—usually at the worst possible moment, when the cost of being wrong has already been paid.

A genuinely productive meeting may look quite different. It might end not with consensus but with clarity about disagreement: a precise statement of what people actually disagree about, a shared understanding of what evidence would settle the question, and a named person responsible for gathering that evidence. This is a harder standard than it sounds, and it requires us to rethink what we mean by progress.
